questions.question: A health care worker has been found to be seropositive for HBsAg, HBeAg, and anti-HBc IgM, indicating an acute HBV infection with high infectivity. A liver biopsy in such cases is likely to show all the following except:

explanation.text: Ground glass hepatocytes are hepatocytes with a granular, eosinophilic cytoplasm. This appearance is due to the accumulation of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) within the endoplasmic reticulum of hepatocytes. This feature is more characteristic of chronic HBV infection rather than acute infection. It reflects ongoing viral replication and chronicity.

Incorrect Options: Options A, C, and D A. Ballooning change of hepatocytes: Common in acute hepatitis. C. Focal or spotty necrosis: Common in acute hepatitis. D. Confluent necrosis of hepatocytes: Seen in severe acute hepatitis.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man is found to have hepatomegaly on physical examination. He also complains of having dark tan skin despite avoiding sun exposure. His liver microscopy is given on the slide below. What is this patient most likely suffering from?

explanation.text: The patient's presentation with dark tan skin and histopathological findings showing iron deposition in liver cells is suggestive of hemochromatosis. Hemochromatosis is a hereditary disorder characterized by the accumulation of iron in the body, which can lead to damage to various organs, including the liver, heart, and pancreas.

Incorrect Options: Option A - Wilson's disease: Wilson's disease is an inherited disorder that causes copper to accumulate in various organs, including the liver, brain, and eyes. The symptoms of Wilson's disease usually begin in childhood or early adulthood and can include neurological symptoms such as tremors, dystonia, and difficulty with coordination. The liver damage associated with Wilson's disease can lead to hepatomegaly, as well as signs of liver disease such as jaundice, ascites, and elevated liver enzymes.

Option B - Autoimmune hepatitis: Autoimmune hepatitis is a chronic autoimmune disorder that causes inflammation and damage to the liver. The symptoms of autoimmune hepatitis can include fatigue, joint pain, skin rashes, and abdominal pain. Liver damage can lead to hepatomegaly, as well as signs of liver disease such as jaundice, ascites, and elevated liver enzymes.

Option C - α-1 antitrypsin deficiency: α-1 antitrypsin deficiency is a genetic disorder that affects the production of a protein called α-1 antitrypsin, which plays a role in protecting the lungs and liver from damage. The symptoms of α-1 antitrypsin deficiency can include respiratory symptoms such as shortness of breath and coughing, as well as liver diseases such as hepatomegaly and elevated liver enzymes.

questions.question: Chronic viral hepatitis is seen with all of the following viruses, except?

explanation.text: The hepatitis E virus causes an acute self-limiting infection. HEV is mainly transmitted through the fecal-oral route and is commonly associated with acute hepatitis.
Incorrect Options: Options A, B, and C can lead to chronic hepatitis.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man is found to have hepatomegaly on physical examination. He also complains of a dark tan despite avoiding sun exposure. His liver microscopy is given on the slide below. This patient most likely suffers from which condition?

explanation.text: Hemochromatosis is a genetic disorder characterized by excessive iron absorption and accumulation in various organs, including the liver. Hepatomegaly is a common finding in hemochromatosis due to iron deposition in hepatocytes. The liver microscopy image showing hepatocellular iron staining supports the diagnosis of hemochromatosis in this patient.
Darkening of the skin, known as bronze diabetes or dark tan, is another characteristic feature of hemochromatosis resulting from iron deposition in the skin.

Incorrect Options: Option A - Wilson's disease: Wilson's disease is a genetic disorder characterized by impaired copper transport, leading to copper accumulation in various organs, including the liver and brain. It typically presents with hepatic and neurological symptoms, such as hepatomegaly, jaundice, and neurologic manifestations.

Option B - Autoimmune hepatitis: Autoimmune hepatitis is an autoimmune disorder characterized by immune-mediated inflammation of the liver. It can present with hepatomegaly, jaundice, and elevated liver enzymes.

Option C - Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is a genetic disorder that predisposes individuals to liver and lung diseases. Liver involvement in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency typically presents as neonatal cholestasis or later-onset liver disease.

questions.question: All of these are characteristic features of pancreatic carcinoma, except:

options.A: Cigarette smoking is a risk factor
options.B: Carcinoma of body pancreas often present with jaundice

explanation.text: Carcinomas of the body and tail of the pancreas often do not present with jaundice because they are not located near the common bile duct. Jaundice is more commonly associated with tumors located in the head of the pancreas, where they can obstruct the common bile duct and lead to the accumulation of bilirubin in the bloodstream.
In contrast, tumors in the body of the pancreas may cause symptoms such as abdominal pain, weight loss, and digestive issues but are less likely to cause jaundice.

Incorrect Options: Option A - Cigarette smoking is a risk factor: Cigarette smoking is a well-established risk factor for pancreatic carcinoma. It is one of the most significant environmental risk factors for developing pancreatic cancer, increasing the likelihood of developing the disease.

Option C - They elicit intense desmoplastic response: Pancreatic carcinoma is known for its intense desmoplastic response. The tumor microenvironment in pancreatic cancer is characterized by the proliferation of fibrous connective tissue, which creates a dense stromal reaction around the tumor cells. This desmoplastic response contributes to the poor prognosis and therapeutic challenges associated with pancreatic carcinoma.

Option D - Perineural invasion is common: Perineural invasion is a common feature of pancreatic carcinoma. The tumor cells have a propensity to invade and infiltrate along the nerves in the vicinity of the pancreas, which can contribute to the spread and metastasis of the disease.

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) is true?

options.A: The GBM is primarily composed of collagen type I and elastin.
options.B: The GBM is a selective barrier between the glomerular capillaries and Bowman's capsule.
options.C: Thickening of the GBM is a characteristic feature of minimal change disease.
options.D: The GBM is impermeable to large molecules such as albumin.

explanation.text: Option B accurately describes the function of the GBM, which acts as a semipermeable barrier, allowing small molecules to pass while restricting the passage of larger molecules, such as proteins, thereby facilitating urine formation.

GBM primarily comprises collagen type IV, laminins, proteoglycans, and other glycoproteins.(Option A) Thickening of the GBM is associated with conditions such as diabetic nephropathy and membranous nephropathy, but not minimal change disease, which typically shows normal or minimal changes in the GBM under light microscopy.(Option C) GBM is permeable to small molecules but is a selective barrier to larger molecules such as albumin. (Option D)

Putty kidney refers to the appearance of the kidney in advanced renal tuberculosis, characterised by caseous necrosis. ( Option A) A leather-grain kidney appearance is seen in benign hypertension. ( Option B) A Waxy kidney is seen in advanced amyloidosis..( Option D)

questions.question: A 60-year-old female presents with a history of recurrent urinary tract infections and lower abdominal pain. Upon physical examination, palpable masses are noted in the pelvis. Urinalysis reveals persistent pyuria. A biopsy was done on the bladder lesions, which is shown below. Which of the following conditions is most likely responsible for the patient's presentation?

explanation.text: Malakoplakia: Acquired defects in phagocyte function. It arises in chronic bacterial infection, mostly by E. coli Morphology: Cystoscopically, malakoplakia takes the form of soft yellow, slightly raised mucosal plaques, 3 to 4 cm in diameter. Histologically, the lesion comprises aggregates of large foamy macrophages known as Hansmann Cells.
The laminated mineralised concretions from calcium deposition in enlarged lysosomes, known as Michaelis-Gutmann bodies, are typically present within the macrophages.

Bladder carcinoma typically would reveal malignant cells.( Option A) Schistosomiasis can cause chronic granulomatous inflammation in the bladder wall, leading to fibrosis and calcification.( Option C) Tubercular cystitis reveals caseating granulomas with Langhans giant cells and epithelioid cells.( Option D)

explanation.text: Characteristics ADPKD ARPKD Affected age group Adults Children Cysts Are present in both outer and inner surfaces Present only on the inner surface. questions.question: Match the following types of renal crystals with their characteristics Types of Renal Crystals Characteristics 1. Calcium Oxalate Monohydrate A. Coffin lid-shaped crystals, commonly found in alkaline urine 2.. Uric Acid B. Rhomboid-shaped crystals, typically seen in acidic urine. 3. Cystine C. Dumbbell or ovoid-shaped crystals are often colourless in acidic urine. 4.. Struvite (Magnesium Ammonium Phosphate) D. Hexagonal plates, often associated with acidic urine

explanation.text: The microscopic appearance of various types of crystals and their descriptions are given below: Struvite/ Staghorn stones: Radioopaque. Seen in alkaline urine. Rectangular/coffin lid appearance. Associated with urea-splitting organisms. Cystine Stones Radiopaque. Seen in acidic urine. Hexagonal Shaped. Very hard stones. Calcium Oxalate Monohydrate stones Radiopaque. Seen in acidic urine. Dumbell shaped. Most common type of renal calculi.
Uric Acid crystals Radiolucent. Seen in acidic urine. Rhomboids or parallelograms. Ammonium Urate crystals Radiolucent. Associated with laxative abuse.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman presents with complaints of severe lower abdominal pain, dysuria, and hematuria. She has a history of recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs). Urinalysis reveals a high pH of 8.5 and the presence of white blood cells. Microscopic examination of the urine sediment shows the following finding. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of the patient's current presentation?

explanation.text: Triple phosphate stones, also known as struvite stones, are composed of magnesium ammonium phosphate. They typically form in alkaline urine due to urinary tract infections caused by urease-producing bacteria. These bacteria hydrolyse urea into ammonia, increasing urine pH and facilitating stone formation. Struvite stones are characterised by their "coffin lid" appearance under a microscope.
They can grow rapidly and fill the renal pelvis, leading to complications like infection and obstruction.

questions.question: A 45-year-old male presents with confusion, nausea, and abdominal pain after consuming antifreeze due to stress. Urinalysis reveals elevated BUN and creatinine. Microscopic examination is shown below. Identify the type of cast.

explanation.text: The clinical vignette of a patient with a history of anti-freeze consumption presenting with confusion, nausea, abdominal pain, elevated BUN and creatinine is suggestive of ethylene glycol poisoning. Muddy brown casts will be seen in this condition. Muddy brown casts: They are often seen in patients with ethylene glycol poisoning, leading to acute tubular necrosis (ATN).

Ethylene glycol metabolites can damage renal tubules, resulting in the formation of muddy brown casts in urine sediment.. The dark brown colouration is due to haemoglobin breakdown products and other cellular components.

questions.question: All of the following are true about medullary sponge kidney except:

options.A: It is more common in adults.
options.B: It is characterised by dilated collecting ducts in the renal medulla.
options.C: It often presents with recurrent urinary tract infections.
options.D: Cysts are lined by cuboidal epithelium.

explanation.text: Medullary Sponge Kidney (MSK) often presents with recurrent urinary tract infections is incorrect because recurrent UTIs are not a defining feature of the condition. While patients with MSK may experience urinary tract infections, it is not a characteristic or common presentation of the disease. It is usually asymptomatic.

Medullary Sponge Kidney: The term medullary sponge kidney is restricted to multiple cystic dilations of the collecting ducts in the medulla. The condition occurs in adults and is usually discovered radiographically. (Option A). Renal function is usually normal.

**On gross inspection, the papillary ducts in the medulla are dilated (Option B):** and small cysts may be present. The cysts are lined by cuboidal epithelium or occasionally by transitional epithelium. (Option D). Unless there is superimposed pyelonephritis, cortical scarring is absent. The pathogenesis is unknown.

questions.question: A 12-year-old male child presents to the clinic with a history of progressive hearing loss, blurred vision, and recurrent episodes of hematuria over the past few months.Electron microscopy reveals the ‘basketweave’ appearance of GBM. Which of the following morphological findings is responsible for this appearance?

options.B: Thickening of the glomerular basement membrane with subepithelial electron-dense deposits
options.C: Irregular thickening, thinning, and splitting of the glomerular basement membrane
options.D: Mesangial expansion with GBM thickening and eosinophilic nodular glomerulosclerosis

explanation.text: The clinical presentation and EM findings of the characteristic basket-weave appearance of GBM suggest Alport syndrome arises due to mutations affecting type IV collagen, resulting in hematuria progressing to chronic renal insufficiency. It presents alongside sensorineural hearing impairment and various ocular manifestations, including lens subluxation, posterior subcapsular cataracts, and corneal dystrophy.

Histologically, Alport syndrome shows distinct electron microscopic features: GBM exhibits irregular areas of thickening interspersed with thinning. Splitting and layering of the lamina densa (basket-weave appearance of GBM) Effacement of podocyte foot processes (Option A) Effacement of podocytes is characteristically seen in Minimal change disease, not the Alport syndrome.

**Thickening of the glomerular basement membrane with subepithelial electron-dense deposits (Option B):** Membranous nephropathy shows the thickening of the glomerular basement membrane without hypercellularity on light microscopy, while electron microscopy shows the ‘spike and dome’ appearance of subepithelial deposits.

**Mesangial expansion with GBM thickening and eosinophilic nodular glomerulosclerosis (Option D):** Diabetic glomerulonephropathy shows mesangial expansion with GBM thickening and eosinophilic nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions)

questions.question: A 55-year-old patient with a history of poorly controlled diabetes presents with worsening kidney function. Upon examination, renal biopsy reveals glomerular changes consistent with diabetic nephropathy. Which histological findings would be least likely to be observed in the glomeruli of this patient's kidney biopsy?

explanation.text: In uncontrolled diabetes, glucosuria causes glycogen accumulation in the proximal tubular cells (not in the glomerulus), known as Armanni-Ebstein cells. This pathological finding is more commonly associated with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) than with diabetic nephropathy. Incorrect options

questions.question: A 32-year-old female presents with a history of joint pain, skin rash, and recent onset of shortness of breath. Lab investigations reveal elevated anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies and low complement levels. A kidney biopsy shows >50% involvement of glomeruli with wire loop lesions on light microscopy. Which type of lupus nephritis is most likely observed in the biopsy findings?

explanation.text: Based on the clinical scenario and lab results, the patient likely has systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) with renal involvement. The kidney biopsy revealing >50% glomerular involvement with wire loop lesions indicates class IV lupus nephritis, the most common and severe form.

Classification of Lupus Nephritis (LN): Class I Minimal Mesangial LN Class II Mesangial proliferative LN Class III (Option A) Focal LN (<50% glomeruli) Class IV Diffuse LN (>50% glomeruli) Class V (Option C) Membranous LN Class VI (Option D) Advanced Sclerosing LN Light microscopy: Subendothelial immune complex deposits can result in the circumferential thickening of the capillary wall, leading to the formation of "wire loop" structures, which are observed in Class III, IV (maximum) and V. Electron microscopy: Thumbprint/ fingerprint sign (alternating areas of electron-dense deposits and lucent regions in GBM, indicating immune complex deposition) Immunofluorescence: Full House Effect (IgG, IgA, IgM, C1, C3 get deposited in the kidney)

questions.question: A 45-year-old male presents with generalised oedema and frothy urine. Laboratory investigations reveal significant proteinuria and hypoalbuminemia. A kidney biopsy reveals diffuse thickening of GBM, a spike and dome pattern on the silver stain and subepithelial deposits on electron microscopy. Which of the following genetic mutations is most likely associated with this condition?

explanation.text: The clinical presentation, along with the histological findings of diffuse thickening of GBM, a spike and dome pattern on the silver stain, and subepithelial deposits on electron microscopy, suggest Membranous nephropathy, the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in elderly patients. In primary membranous nephropathy, antibodies primarily target the M-type phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R) located on the basal surface of podocytes.

This triggers complement activation and subepithelial immune complex deposition, resembling Heymann nephritis lesions. Other less common target antigens include THSD7A and neutral endopeptidase (CD10). The presence of anti-PLA2R antibodies is crucial for diagnosing the disease.

questions.question: A 25-year-old female presents with edema, hypertension, significant proteinuria, and hematuria. Kidney biopsy reveals mesangial and endocapillary hypercellularity with mesangial and subendothelial electron-dense deposits, tram track appearance on silver stains and granular staining for IgG and C3 on Immunofluorescence. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: Tram track or double contour appearance due to splitting of GBM Pathology Light Microscope Electron Microscope Immunofluorescence Type I MPGN (Option A) Mesangial proliferative or membranoproliferative patterns of proliferation; GBM thickening and Splitting. (Double-contour or tram track appearance) Subendothelial and mesangial deposits IgG ++ C3 (C1q ++ C4 may also present) Type II MPGN (Dense Deposit Disease) (Option B) Dense intramembranous deposits C3; no C1q or C4 Membranous Nephropathy (Option C) Diffuse capillary wall thickening Subepithelial deposits Granular IgG and C3; diffuse Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) (Option D) Focal and segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis Effacement of foot processes; epithelial denudation Focal; IgM + C3 in many cases

questions.question: Which genetic mutation is responsible for a syndrome of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome of childhood onset?

explanation.text: The above clinical scenario points towards the diagnosis of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome, which is defined as the absence of remission despite 4 weeks of therapy with daily prednisone at a dose of 2 mg/kg/d. Mutations in the NPHS2 gene lead to this syndrome, typically manifesting in childhood. The NPHS2 gene is located on chromosome 1q25–q31.

The NPHS2 gene encodes the protein product known as podocin which is localised to the slit diaphragm within the kidney. Patients typically present from birth to 6 years of age have a steroid-resistant course and reach End-stage Renal Disease (ESRD) before the end of their first decade.

**NPHS1 (Option A):** NPHS1 mutations are associated with congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type. α-actinin 4 (Option C) Mutations in the gene encoding the podocyte actin-binding protein α-actinin 4 (ACTN4) underlie some cases of autosomal dominant focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), which tends to have a high rate of progression to renal insufficiency.

**TRPC6 (Option D):** Mutations in the TRPC6 gene, which encodes a calcium-permeable ion channel in podocytes, have been identified in some cases of familial FSGS. However, TRPC6 mutations are not typically linked to childhood-onset steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome.
